title: The story so far
intro_md: How Phobos got here. Dates are US Eastern.

chapters.title: Roots in ares, higan and bsnes
paras_md: Phobos started from [ares](https://github.com/ares-emulator/ares), which goes back through [higan](https://github.com/higan-emu/higan) to [bsnes](https://github.com/bsnes-emu/bsnes) in 2004. ares puts accuracy first and trades some speed for clear code.
Phobos keeps the cores that way and adds faster paths around them. None of it would exist without Near, the ares team and everyone credited below.

chapters.title: Taking it to Android

quote.text_md: It started off as a desktop to Android port of ares

paras_md: ares is a desktop program. Phobos forked it in July 2026 and took it to Android, swapping ares's desktop front end for a Kotlin and Jetpack Compose app.
The N64 recompilers and Vulkan renderer got ARM64 work, and v1.0.0 came out on 20 August 2026 with the Neo Geo core and a GPU Driver Manager for Mesa's Turnip driver.

chapters.title: A faster N64 and a new look
paras_md: On 15 September we set the ground rules. Speed claims need a measurement, and changes need an independent review before they merge.
Then came four days on the N64, all measured on my Retroid Pocket 6. Dispatcher trips fell from 10.1 to 0.6 million a second (#10), and a Mario Tennis scene went from 82 late frames to 5 (#17).
The app got its look at the same time, with 37 themes (#9), a performance overlay (#5) and a glass dock (#20). v1.1.0 came out on 28 September.
On 29 September we put a PSP core on the plan, one to rival PPSSPP in compatibility and speed.

chapters.title: A clean-room PSP core
paras_md: Phobos couldn't adopt PPSSPP. It's under the GPL, and the console firmware ares compiles in can't be. So on 3 October Phobos started a PSP core from scratch, using PPSSPP only to learn how the PSP behaves, with nothing copied, translated or reworded.
By 6 October, the first 3D games reached gameplay and a headless runner had put all 266 test games through a minute each (#154). A Vulkan renderer followed on 7 October.
Library runs went round and round until only one game of 266 stayed black. v2.0.0 shipped the core on 11 October as Experimental, with 194 of the 266 reaching a menu or gameplay in its final run.

On 16 October I timed real games' display lists on my PSP-1000. They took a hell of a lot longer than Phobos's model charged, 4 to 12 times as long. After more rounds, the measured timing became the default on 19 October (#269).

chapters.title: Back to the desktop

quote.text_md: Has since merged back to desktop in an attempt to port it back to allow for easier controller navigation/use, as well as a sleek, modern UI.

paras_md: On 3 October the cores came back to the desktop on Linux, macOS and Windows, with CI building them for every pull request (#97). The PSP joined on 6 October.
The desktop program is pretty plain for now, drawn in SDL's debug font. Like I said above, the goal is to bring the Android app's easy controller navigation and sleek, modern UI to the desktop.
The library and menus already work with a gamepad, and #294 brought hotkeys to the desktop on 23 October, with a Hotkeys page in the pause menu.
